extracted.intended_audience: trademark applicants and their attorneys; U.S. Trademark Examining Attorneys; practitioners before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules governing amendments, requests to divide, statements of use, and submission of evidence during ex parte appeals to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, including remand and ESTTA/TEAS filing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment filed within six months accompanying notice of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: If, within six months following the issuance of a final action (or a second refusal on the same ground(s) or repeated requirement), an applicant files both an amendment to its application and an ex parte appeal, the applicant should indicate in its notice of appeal that it has also filed an amendment; if filing through ESTTA, check the box indicating a request for reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will acknowledge receipt, suspend proceedings (including time to file the appeal brief), and remand the application to the examining attorney to consider the amendment. The Board's remand letter will include instructions for the examining attorney. The examining attorney may attempt to resolve outstanding issues and may submit evidence relevant to the amendment but may not assert a new refusal or requirement unrelated to the amendment unless the examining attorney files a request under 37 CFR § 2.142(f)(6) for remand to assert the new refusal or requirement and that request is granted. See TBMP § 1204, TBMP § 1203.02(a), and TMEP § 715.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant should not file appeal brief pending remand/order
rubrics_metrics.description: If the notice of appeal is filed by paper and the applicant has also timely filed an amendment but has not heard from the Board within sixty days regarding the appeal and amendment, the applicant should not file its appeal brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may assume the Board will institute the appeal, suspend proceedings and remand the application to the examining attorney, in which event the due date for the appeal brief will be reset if the amendment does not place the application in condition for publication or registration. The applicant does not need to verify with the Board that the due date will be changed. See TBMP § 1203.02(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining attorney may approve application after amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examining attorney is persuaded, on the basis of the amendment, that the applicant is entitled to the registration sought, the examining attorney may approve the application for publication or registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If approved, the appeal will be moot and the examining attorney should notify the applicant by telephone or e-mail. See TMEP § 715.04 and TMEP § 1501.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of amendment but adherence to final refusal — office action content and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examining attorney accepts the amendment but adheres to the final refusal because other grounds remain or the amendment does not obviate the refusal, the examining attorney should issue a written action indicating acceptance of the amendment and what refusals/requirements remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six‑month response clause should be omitted from that paper; the application should be returned to the Board; proceedings with respect to the appeal will be resumed; and the applicant will be allowed time to file its appeal brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: If amendment raises a new issue — nonfinal action required
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examining attorney refuses to accept the amendment and the amendment raises a new issue, the examining attorney must allow the applicant an opportunity to respond before issuing a final refusal and returning the application to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, the first Office action that considers and refuses the amendment must be a nonfinal action and must include the six-month response clause. See TBMP § 1201.02 and TMEP §§ 714.05 et seq., 715.04(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments filed more than six months after final action treated as request for remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant files an amendment more than six months after issuance of the final action (or second refusal or repeated requirement) from which the appeal was taken, the Board will treat the amendment as a request for remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a request will be granted upon a showing of good cause. Whether good cause exists depends in part on the stage of the appeal and the reason for the delay. Examples of good cause include attempts to comply with a requirement (e.g., acceptable identification) or to obviate a ground for refusal (e.g., asserting § 2(f) claim to avoid § 2(e) refusal). See TBMP § 1209.04; In re Thomas White Int’l Ltd., 106 USPQ2d 1158 (TTAB 2013) (late amendment not good cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board discretion to refuse remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Remand in an ex parte appeal is discretionary; the Board may refuse to remand for amendments filed more than six months after the action or filed after the examining attorney acted following a notice of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remand may be refused if the amendment was filed in bad faith or would serve no useful purpose. If remand is made, the Board's instructions to the examining attorney may differ depending on when the amendment was filed (e.g., at the point the examining attorney’s brief is due the Board may direct limited handling such as noting acceptance in the briefs). See In re Big Pig Inc., 81 USPQ2d 1436 (TTAB 2006); In re HerbalScience Group LLC, 96 USPQ2d 1321 (TTAB 2010).

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-filed appeal with timely amendment — procedural consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If an appeal is late-filed but the applicant timely filed an amendment to its involved application, the Board will issue a written action informing the applicant of the lateness of its appeal and forwarding the application to the examining attorney for appropriate action with respect to the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The late appeal will not be entertained by the Board; the examining attorney will handle the amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment included in appeal brief — treated as request for remand
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant files its appeal brief and also wishes to amend the application (e.g., to comply with a requirement or overcome a refusal), the proper procedure is to file a request for remand and request suspension pending the Board’s decision; an amendment included in a brief will be treated as a request for remand if noted by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Board does not note the proposed amendment but the examining attorney, upon reviewing the brief, allows it, the amendment will be entered; preferred practice is for the examining attorney to state in his/her brief that the amendment is accepted. If the examining attorney believes the amendment raises a new issue, the examining attorney should contact the Board to have the amendment treated as a request for remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment after decision
rubrics_metrics.description: An application that has been considered and decided on appeal may be amended, if at all, only in accordance with 37 CFR § 2.142(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For further information see TBMP § 1218 and TMEP § 1501.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request to divide (general allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may submit a request to divide the application to divide out goods or services within a class, or entire classes, prior to, with, or after the filing of a notice of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A request to divide may be used where a refusal/requirement applies only to certain classes or certain goods/services within a class. If submitted after an appeal is instituted, the request should be filed with the Board (not with the examining attorney or through TEAS). The Board will determine whether to suspend action on the appeal and forward the application to the ITU/Divisional Unit or defer processing and continue proceedings; the determination is based on factors such as the reason for division and the stage of the appeal. Filing via ESTTA is strongly encouraged. See 37 CFR § 2.87 and TMEP § 1110.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request to divide — ESTTA electronic filing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a notice of appeal is submitted through ESTTA and a request to divide is pending or filed contemporaneously, the applicant should not check the 'request for reconsideration' box unless a request for reconsideration/amendment is also pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The request to divide is not a request for reconsideration or amendment. The notice of appeal should be filed through ESTTA and the request to divide through TEAS. The applicant will receive an order instituting the appeal and will be asked to contact the Board paralegal for processing. Outcomes: if appeal limited to classes to be divided out, appeal instituted for those classes, proceedings suspended, application forwarded to ITU/Divisional Unit; after processing, applications handled appropriately and applicant allowed 60 days to submit its appeal brief; Board may consolidate appeals. See TBMP § 1214.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request to divide — paper filing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a notice of appeal is filed as a paper submission and a request to divide is also filed or pending, the applicant should advise the Board of the request to divide in the notice of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If request to divide is the only pending paper, the Board will institute the appeal, suspend proceedings and forward the application to the ITU/Divisional Unit for action. If the appeal applies to only one of the resulting applications, that application will be returned to the Board after processing and the applicant will have 60 days to submit its appeal brief; if applies to both, Board may resume action on both and may consolidate. If a request to divide and request for reconsideration/amendment are filed together, the Board will remand to the examining attorney to process the division then decide the reconsideration/amendment in the normal manner. Applicant may not later file a notice of appeal for classes for which it had not previously filed a timely notice of appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to allege use (§ 1(c)) timing
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to allege use under Trademark Act § 1(c) may be filed in an intent‑to‑use application at any time between the filing of the application and the date the examining attorney approves the mark for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thereafter, an allegation of use may be submitted only as a statement of use under § 1(d) after issuance of a notice of allowance. Thus an amendment to allege use filed during the pendency of an ex parte appeal is timely. See 37 CFR § 2.76(a); TMEP §§ 1104.03, 1104.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling amendment to allege use filed with an appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: If an amendment to allege use is filed during the six‑month response period and the applicant also files a timely appeal and the examining attorney has not acted on the amendment when the appeal is filed, the amendment will be handled the same as any other amendment filed during the six‑month response period following issuance of a final action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing notice of appeal through ESTTA, check the request for reconsideration box and file the amendment through TEAS; ESTTA filing will generate an order instituting the appeal, suspending action, and remanding the application to the examining attorney to consider the amendment to allege use. Applicant should not file its appeal brief within sixty days. If examining attorney approves for publication or the application is abandoned, the appeal will be moot and the examining attorney should notify the applicant. If examining attorney adheres to final refusal or issues a new final refusal, omit six‑month clause, return application to the Board and resume appeal. See TBMP § 1205 and TMEP § 1104.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of use (§ 1(d)) premature filing rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of use under Trademark Act § 1(d) is premature if filed in an intent‑to‑use application prior to issuance of a notice of allowance under § 13(b)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement of use filed during an ex parte appeal is generally premature, will not be considered, and will be returned to the applicant with a refund of the fee. See 37 CFR § 2.88(a); TMEP § 1109.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule — evidence submitted after appeal is untimely
rubrics_metrics.description: The record in the application should be complete prior to filing an appeal; the TTAB will ordinarily not consider additional evidence filed with the Board by the appellant or examiner after the appeal is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If party desires to introduce additional evidence after appeal is filed, the proper procedure is to request the Board to suspend the appeal and remand the application for further examination. Numerous TTAB cases hold new evidence submitted with reply or appeal briefs is untimely and not considered (collect citations listed). See 37 CFR § 2.142(d) and TBMP § 1203.02(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — submission of complete article by nonoffering party
rubrics_metrics.description: If one party submitted excerpts from articles during examination, the nonoffering party may submit the complete article after appeal is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better practice is to submit the full article with a request for remand. However, because the party submitting the excerpt had the opportunity to review the entire article, if the article is submitted with an appeal brief the Board need not remand and may consider the article as part of the record. Cf. In re Psygnosis Ltd., 51 USPQ2d 1594 (TTAB 1999) (but other holdings treat such submissions as additional evidence and untimely). See TBMP § 1208.01 and case law cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request to remand for additional evidence — filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A request under 37 CFR § 2.142(d) to suspend and remand for additional evidence must be filed prior to the Board's final decision, include a showing of good cause (satisfactory explanation for why the evidence was not filed prior to appeal), and be accompanied by the additional evidence sought to be introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The length of delay after the reason for remand becomes known and the point in the appeal process when the request is made will be considered in determining good cause; generally, the later in the appeal the stronger the reason that must be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of circumstances constituting good cause for remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances found to constitute good cause include: (1) the evidence was not previously available (but not merely cumulative); (2) a new attorney for the applicant or a new examining attorney has taken over the case (with limited caveats); (3) the applicant and examining attorney have agreed to the remand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if evidence was not previously available, good cause may be denied if the evidence is merely cumulative. Transfer among firm members is not good cause; transfer from in‑house counsel to an outside firm is treated as a new attorney. Consent agreements in § 2(d) refusals are treated as inherently difficult and persuasive; the Board will grant remand for consideration of a consent agreement if filed at any time prior to the Board's final decision, if accompanied by the consent agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences if remand for additional evidence is granted — right to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: If a request to remand for additional evidence is granted, the nonrequesting party may submit additional evidence in response to the evidence submitted with the request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on the stage of the appeal, the Board may direct that any responsive evidence be submitted with a supplemental brief. See TBMP § 1209.02 and TBMP § 1209.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examining attorney actions after remand for additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is remanded for further examination the examining attorney may approve the application for publication/registration, adhere to the action from which the appeal was taken, or issue a new nonfinal action asserting any new refusal or requirement necessitated by the new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examining attorney may not assert a new refusal or requirement unrelated to the new evidence unless he/she files a request under 37 CFR § 2.142(f)(6) for remand to assert the new refusal and the request is granted. If the examining attorney approves registration based on new evidence, the appeal is moot and the examining attorney should notify the applicant. If the examining attorney adheres or issues a new final refusal, omit six‑month clause, return to Board, and resume appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board procedure when examining attorney requests remand and request is granted
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examining attorney's request to suspend and remand for additional evidence is granted, the Board will allow the examining attorney time to issue an Office action (with no six‑month response clause) relating to the new evidence to be submitted therewith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the examining attorney's new action is issued the application is returned to the Board and proceedings on the appeal are resumed. The applicant will be allowed an opportunity to submit responsive evidence and, if the applicant's appeal brief has already been filed, to file a supplemental brief directed to the new evidence submitted by the examining attorney.
